# How to use this guide

Cosmetic Science is **one of the semester-8 electives** of the PCI B.Pharm course. It has no practical; the whole subject is the 75-mark theory paper. The subject is descriptive with almost no calculations (SPF is the only formula you must write). Marks come from clear definitions, ingredient tables ("building blocks"), mechanisms and labelled diagrams. Study one unit a day: read the notes, write each formula table and mechanism once from memory, draw the diagrams (skin layers, hair cross-section, PPD dye reaction, antiperspirant plug, instrument principles), then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus. The syllabus lists antiperspirants and deodorants in both Unit II and Unit V; in this guide Unit 2 gives a short summary and the full topic is in Unit 5. Indian cosmetic law (Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Cosmetics Rules, 2020) is covered in Unit 1 with the definition of cosmetics. Cold cream, vanishing cream, shampoo, toothpaste, hair dye and sunscreen basics were first met in Industrial Pharmacy I (BP502T, Unit 5); this guide builds on them, so revise both together.

Formulas in the notes are **typical examples** to show the role of each ingredient. In the exam, a table of ingredient, role and example (with an approximate range if you know it) earns full marks; you do not need to memorise exact quantities.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a table, a diagram and examples.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Cosmetics and basics | Definition of cosmetics (Indian and EU), cosmeceuticals, quasi and OTC drugs, classification of excipients (surfactants, humectants, emollients, preservatives, rheology modifiers), structure of skin and hair, hair growth cycle, oral problems |
| 2 Formulation | Cold cream vs vanishing cream, moisturising cream, face wash, conditioning and anti-dandruff shampoo, hair conditioner, hair oils, PPD hair dye chemistry, toothpaste for sensitive teeth and bleeding gums, whitening, mouthwash |
| 3 Sun, herbs, analysis | UVA/UVB, classification of sunscreens, SPF and its determination, aloe, turmeric, henna, amla, neem, clove, BIS tests for shampoo, cream and toothpaste |
| 4 Evaluation, soaps | Sebumeter, corneometer, TEWL, skin colour, hair tensile strength, combing, soap vs syndet bar |
| 5 Skin and hair problems | Dry and oily skin, moisturisation, comedogenic, dermatitis, dandruff, hair fall, acne, wrinkles, blemishes, prickly heat, body odour, antiperspirants vs deodorants |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Start with a one-line definition, then a **building-blocks table** (ingredient – role – example). This one habit covers most formulation questions in Units 2 and 5.
2. For every formulation, add the **method** in 4–5 arrows and 3–4 **evaluation tests**; examiners look for all three parts.
3. Draw: skin layers, hair shaft cross-section, hair growth cycle, PPD oxidation scheme, antiperspirant plug, sebumeter and TEWL probe principle, stress–strain curve of hair.
4. Learn the exact facts the paper can test: UVB 290–320 nm, UVA 320–400 nm; SPF = MED protected ÷ MED unprotected at 2 mg/cm²; water's dielectric constant about 80 (corneometer); TEWL in g/m²/h; skin surface pH about 4.5–5.5; soap pH 9–10, syndet 5.5–7; BIS toilet soap TFM grades 76/70/60%; henna – lawsone; clove – eugenol; turmeric – curcumin.
5. In law questions, quote the Indian definition from the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and name the Cosmetics Rules, 2020; do not invent rule or form numbers.
6. For comparison questions (cold vs vanishing cream, soap vs syndet, physical vs chemical sunscreen, antiperspirant vs deodorant, irritant vs allergic dermatitis) use a two-column table with at least six points.
7. In problem-based questions (dandruff, acne, hair fall, dry skin) write: definition → causes → cosmetic approach with named actives → when to see a doctor.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers with a table or diagram each: **cold cream vs vanishing cream (with building blocks)**, **sunscreens: classification and SPF**, **PPD hair dye chemistry and formulation**, **antiperspirants and deodorants**, and **sebumeter, corneometer and TEWL**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Definitions in one line**

| Term | One-line meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Cosmetic (India) | Article rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed, introduced or applied to the body to cleanse, beautify, promote attractiveness or alter appearance, including components (D&C Act, 1940) |
| Cosmetic (EU) | Substance or mixture placed on external body parts, teeth or oral mucosa mainly to clean, perfume, change appearance, protect, keep in good condition or correct body odour (Regulation 1223/2009) |
| Cosmeceutical | Cosmetic with an active claimed to give a biological benefit; not a legal category |
| Quasi drug | Japanese category of medicated cosmetics (anti-dandruff, whitening, deodorant) |
| Humectant | Hygroscopic agent that attracts and holds water (glycerin, sorbitol, sodium PCA) |
| Emollient | Softens and smooths skin (esters, oils, silicones) |
| SPF | MED of protected skin ÷ MED of unprotected skin |
| MED | Smallest UV dose giving just-visible redness after 16–24 h |
| TEWL | Water passing through the epidermis and evaporating; marker of barrier function |
| Comedogenic | Tends to block pores and form comedones |
| Syndet bar | Cleansing bar of synthetic surfactants (SCI), pH about 5.5–7 |
| TFM | Total fatty matter of soap; BIS grades 1/2/3 = at least 76/70/60% |

**Lists to write without thinking**

| Topic | Items |
| --- | --- |
| Cosmetics Rules, 2020 | Under D&C Act; CDSCO = central authority (import registration, new cosmetics); states licence manufacture; BIS standards; labelling; animal testing banned (since 2014) |
| Excipients (syllabus) | Surfactants, rheology modifiers, humectants, emollients, preservatives |
| Surfactant classes | Anionic (SLS, SLES), cationic (cetrimonium chloride), amphoteric (cocamidopropyl betaine), non-ionic (polysorbates) |
| Skin layers | Epidermis (basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum), dermis, hypodermis |
| Hair layers | Cuticle, cortex, medulla; bonds: disulphide, hydrogen, salt |
| Hair cycle | Anagen (2–7 y, 85–90%), catagen (2–3 wk), telogen (about 3 mo, 10–15%), exogen |
| Oral problems | Plaque, caries, calculus, gingivitis, periodontitis, hypersensitivity, stains, halitosis |
| Moisturiser actions | Occlusion, humectancy, emolliency, barrier repair |
| Conditioning shampoo | SLES + betaine + cationic polymer + silicone → coacervate deposits on dilution |
| Conditioner | Cationic surfactant + fatty alcohol + silicone, pH 4–5 |
| Anti-dandruff actives | Zinc pyrithione, ketoconazole, selenium sulphide, piroctone olamine, climbazole, salicylic acid, coal tar |
| PPD dye | PPD (precursor) + coupler (resorcinol) + H2O2 + ammonia → indo dye; patch test 48 h |
| Sensitive teeth | Potassium nitrate (nerve), strontium salts, stannous fluoride, arginine (block tubules) |
| Whitening | Abrasives, H2O2 / carbamide peroxide, blue covarine |
| Mouthwash | Chlorhexidine, CPC, essential oils, fluoride, alcohol or glycols, flavour |
| Sunscreens | Chemical: PABA, cinnamates, salicylates, benzophenones, avobenzone, octocrylene; physical: ZnO, TiO2 |
| UVA rating | PA+ to PA++++, UVA-PF, critical wavelength |
| Herbs | Aloe (acemannan), turmeric (curcumin), henna (lawsone), amla (vitamin C, tannins), neem (azadirachtin, nimbidin), clove (eugenol) |
| Shampoo tests | pH, solids, active matter (two-phase titration), foam (Ross–Miles), wetting, dirt dispersion, heavy metals |
| Cream tests | pH, thermal stability, emulsion type, spreadability, heavy metals, microbial count |
| Toothpaste tests | Abrasive fineness, sharp particles, fluoride (ion-selective electrode, ≤1000 ppm total), pH, heavy metals, stability |
| Instruments | Sebumeter (photometric tape), corneometer (capacitance), Tewameter (open chamber, Fick's law), Mexameter / chromameter (L\*a\*b\*), tensile tester, combing load cell |
| Acne factors | Sebum, plugging, C. acnes, inflammation |
| Hair fall causes | Androgenetic, telogen effluvium, nutrition, thyroid, alopecia areata, drugs, traction and chemicals |

**Key comparisons**

| Cold cream | Vanishing cream |
| --- | --- |
| Mainly w/o | o/w |
| Beeswax + liquid paraffin + borax | Stearic acid + KOH/TEA + glycerin |
| Sodium soap formed in situ | Potassium/TEA stearate |
| Greasy, cooling, cleansing | Matt, non-greasy, pearly, foundation base |

| Antiperspirant | Deodorant |
| --- | --- |
| Reduces sweat | Reduces odour |
| Aluminium chlorohydrate, Al–Zr glycine complexes, AlCl3 | Ethanol, antimicrobials, zinc ricinoleate, perfume |
| Al(OH)3 gel plug in sweat duct | Kills bacteria, absorbs or masks odour |

| Soap | Syndet bar |
| --- | --- |
| Fatty acid salts; pH 9–10 | SCI etc.; pH 5.5–7 |
| Scum in hard water | No scum |
| More lipid loss, higher TEWL | Milder |

**Numbers to remember**

- UVB 290–320 nm; UVA 320–400 nm; SPF test at 2 mg/cm²; SPF 15/30/50 ≈ 93/97/98% UVB blocked.
- Skin surface pH about 4.5–5.5; epidermal turnover about 4 weeks.
- Scalp hair grows about 1 cm per month; up to about 100 hairs shed daily is normal.
- Dielectric constant of water about 80 vs below 7 for other skin substances.
- Instrument tests: rest 15–30 min, about 20–22 °C and 40–60% RH.

**Last tips:** write the building-blocks table for every product, add method and evaluation, draw at least one diagram per long answer, and never invent law numbers or limits.

questions.answer:
1. Indian definition (Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940): any article meant to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, introduced into or otherwise applied to the human body or any part of it for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance; includes articles meant as components of cosmetics.
2. Indian control: Cosmetics Rules, 2020 under the D&C Act; CDSCO is the Central Licensing Authority for import registration and new cosmetics; State Licensing Authorities licence manufacture; BIS standards, labelling, ban on misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics and on animal testing.
3. EU definition (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009): any substance or mixture placed in contact with external parts of the body (epidermis, hair, nails, lips, external genitals) or teeth and oral mucosa, exclusively or mainly to clean, perfume, change appearance, protect, keep in good condition or correct body odour; responsible person, safety report, notification, annexes, animal testing ban.
4. Key point: intended use and claims decide; a disease claim makes a product a drug.
5. Evolution: decorative and traditional cosmetics → modern emulsions and cleansers → functional products (sunscreen, antiperspirant, fluoride paste) → cosmeceuticals with actives (retinol, AHAs, vitamin C, niacinamide, peptides, ceramides); term popularised by Albert Kligman.
6. Drivers: skin biology research, anti-ageing demand, new delivery systems, dermatologist recommendation.
7. Cosmeceutical is not a legal category in India, EU or USA.
8. Quasi drugs: Japanese middle category of medicated cosmetics (anti-dandruff, whitening, anti-acne, deodorant, hair growth) with approved actives and pre-market approval.
9. OTC drugs: in the USA sunscreens, antiperspirants, anti-dandruff shampoos, fluoride toothpastes and anti-acne products are OTC drugs because they prevent disease or affect body function; must follow OTC rules.
10. India has no quasi-drug category: a product is a cosmetic or a drug by its claims and ingredients.
questions.question: Define cosmetics as per Indian and EU regulations. Explain the evolution of cosmeceuticals from cosmetics and discuss cosmetics as quasi drugs and OTC drugs.

questions.answer:
1. Excipients are the building blocks of every cosmetic; the syllabus groups: surfactants, rheology modifiers, humectants, emollients, preservatives (others: antioxidants, chelating agents, pH adjusters, colours, perfumes).
2. Surfactants – amphiphilic molecules lowering surface tension. Anionic: SLS, SLES, soaps (cleansing, foam – shampoo, face wash, toothpaste). Cationic: cetrimonium and behentrimonium chloride (hair conditioners, antimicrobial). Amphoteric: cocamidopropyl betaine (mild, baby shampoo). Non-ionic: polysorbates, sorbitan esters, fatty alcohol ethoxylates (emulsifiers, solubilisers). HLB guides choice: low for w/o, high for o/w.
3. Rheology modifiers – control viscosity and suspension: natural gums (xanthan, guar, carrageenan), cellulose derivatives (Na CMC, HEC, HPMC), carbomers (thicken on neutralisation), clays (bentonite), NaCl (ether sulphate shampoos), fatty alcohols and waxes.
4. Humectants – hygroscopic, attract and hold water in product and skin: glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol, sodium PCA, sodium lactate, urea, hyaluronic acid; combine with occlusives in dry air.
5. Emollients – soften and smooth skin, some occlusive: liquid paraffin, petrolatum, plant oils and butters, esters (isopropyl myristate), fatty alcohols, silicones, lanolin, waxes.
6. Preservatives – prevent microbial growth in water-containing, repeatedly opened products: parabens, phenoxyethanol, benzoic and sorbic acids, formaldehyde releasers, isothiazolinones, benzyl alcohol.
7. Ideal preservative: broad spectrum, low concentration, stable over product pH, compatible, non-irritant, odourless; efficacy checked by challenge test.
8. Applications table: shampoo (surfactant + NaCl + preservative), cream (emollient + emulsifier + humectant + preservative), toothpaste (humectant + binder + SLS), gel (carbomer).

questions.answer:
1. Diagram: epidermis (stratum corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, basale), dermis (papillary, reticular), hypodermis; hair follicle, sebaceous gland, sweat glands, blood vessels.
2. Epidermis: stratified squamous, avascular; keratinocytes formed in basal layer move up and become corneocytes in about four weeks; stratum corneum = barrier ('bricks and mortar': corneocytes + ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids); natural moisturising factor; melanocytes make melanin; Langerhans cells.
3. Dermis: collagen (strength) and elastin (recoil) in glycosaminoglycan gel made by fibroblasts; vessels, nerves, appendages; loss leads to wrinkles.
4. Hypodermis: fat for insulation, cushioning, energy.
5. Appendages: sebaceous glands (sebum), eccrine sweat glands (cooling), apocrine glands (armpit, odour), hair, nails.
6. Functions: protection (mechanical, chemical, microbial, UV), water barrier, temperature control, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, excretion, immunity, appearance; acid mantle pH about 4.5–5.5.
7. Hair structure: shaft and root, bulb around dermal papilla; cuticle (overlapping scales), cortex (keratin, melanin; disulphide, hydrogen and salt bonds), medulla.
8. Hair growth cycle: anagen (growth, 2–7 years, 85–90% of hairs), catagen (2–3 weeks), telogen (rest, about 3 months, 10–15%), exogen (shedding); scalp hair grows about 1 cm per month.
9. Cosmetic relevance: barrier and hydration for moisturisers, melanin for sunscreens and lighteners, cuticle damage and charge for conditioners, cycle for hair fall products.

questions.answer:
1. Surfactants have a hydrophilic head and lipophilic tail; they lower surface and interfacial tension.
2. Anionic (negative head): SLS, SLES, soaps, sodium cocoyl isethionate – strong cleansing and foam; can irritate.
3. Cationic: cetrimonium chloride, behentrimonium chloride, benzalkonium chloride – conditioning (bind negatively charged hair), antimicrobial.
4. Amphoteric: cocamidopropyl betaine – mild, foam booster, baby products.
5. Non-ionic: polysorbates, sorbitan esters, fatty alcohol ethoxylates, alkyl polyglucosides – emulsifiers and solubilisers; low irritation.
6. Functions: cleansing, foaming, emulsifying, wetting, solubilising perfume, conditioning; HLB guides emulsifier choice (3–6 w/o, 8–18 o/w).
questions.question: Write a note on surfactants used in cosmetics with their classification and uses.

questions.answer:
1. Humectants: hygroscopic substances that attract and hold water in the product and the stratum corneum.
2. Examples: glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol, butylene glycol, sodium PCA, sodium lactate, urea, hyaluronic acid.
3. Uses: moisturisers, toothpaste (prevent drying in tube), shampoos, face washes; limitation – in very dry air can draw water from deeper skin, so combined with occlusives.
4. Emollients: soften and smooth skin by filling spaces between surface cells and forming a film; some reduce water loss (occlusive).
5. Examples: liquid paraffin, petrolatum, vegetable oils and butters, esters (isopropyl myristate), fatty alcohols, silicones, lanolin, waxes.
6. Uses: creams, lotions, lipsticks, hair oils, bath oils.
questions.question: Write a short note on humectants and emollients used in cosmetics.

questions.answer:
1. Need: water, nutrients and repeated opening allow bacteria, yeast and mould growth; spoilage and infection risk.
2. Examples: parabens (methyl – bacteria, propyl – fungi), phenoxyethanol, benzoic acid/sodium benzoate and sorbic acid/potassium sorbate (acidic pH), formaldehyde releasers (DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl urea), isothiazolinones (restricted – allergy), benzyl alcohol, dehydroacetic acid.
3. Ideal: broad spectrum, effective at low concentration, stable at product pH, compatible with other ingredients and pack, non-irritant, non-sensitising, colourless and odourless, enough in water phase.
4. Combinations widen spectrum and lower concentrations.
5. Must be within permitted lists and limits (Cosmetics Rules, BIS).
6. Efficacy tested by preservative challenge test.
questions.question: Write a note on preservatives used in cosmetics.

questions.answer:
1. Some products do more than beautify but are sold freely; countries classify them differently.
2. Quasi drugs (Japan): medicated cosmetics with approved actives – anti-dandruff shampoos, whitening products, anti-acne products, deodorants, hair growth products; approval needed but less strict than medicines.
3. OTC drugs (USA): a product preventing disease or affecting body function is a drug – sunscreens, antiperspirants, anti-dandruff shampoos, fluoride toothpastes, anti-acne products; follow OTC rules for actives and labelling; often 'cosmetic–drug'.
4. India and EU: no middle category; such products are cosmetics if claims are cosmetic, drugs if they claim to treat disease (e.g. ketoconazole shampoo is a drug).
5. Significance: claims, labelling and licence depend on category.

questions.answer:
1. Dental plaque: sticky bacterial film; root of most problems.
2. Dental caries: bacterial acids from sugars dissolve enamel → cavities; prevented by fluoride and less sugar.
3. Calculus (tartar): mineralised plaque; anti-tartar pyrophosphates, zinc salts; scaling.
4. Gingivitis: red swollen gums that bleed on brushing; antiplaque agents.
5. Periodontitis: infection reaching bone, loose teeth; dental treatment.
6. Dentine hypersensitivity: pain to cold, heat, sweets when dentine exposed; desensitising pastes.
7. Discolouration: extrinsic stains (tea, coffee, tobacco) and intrinsic; whitening.
8. Halitosis: sulphur compounds from tongue bacteria; tongue cleaning, mouthwash.

questions.answer:
1. Cold cream: cleansing, emollient cream with cooling effect from evaporating water; classic beeswax–borax cream, mainly w/o.
2. Building blocks: white beeswax 12–18% (forms emulsifier, body), liquid paraffin 45–55% (oil, cleansing), borax 0.5–1% (neutralises cerotic acid of beeswax → sodium soap in situ = emulsifier), water 25–35%, perfume, preservative, antioxidant.
3. Method: melt wax and oil at 70–75 °C; dissolve borax in water at same temperature; add aqueous to oil phase with stirring; cool with stirring; perfume near 40 °C; fill.
4. Advantages: cooling, cleanses oil-soluble make-up, good for dry skin, cheap. Disadvantages: greasy, unsuitable for hot humid weather and oily skin, borax restricted in some countries, hard to wash off.
5. Vanishing cream: o/w cream of stearic acid partly neutralised (about one fifth to one quarter) by KOH, NaOH or triethanolamine to form stearate soap; leaves thin matt film and 'vanishes'.
6. Building blocks: stearic acid 15–20%, alkali, glycerin 5–10% (humectant), cetyl alcohol, water, perfume, preservative.
7. Method: melt stearic acid at about 75 °C; dissolve alkali and glycerin in hot water; add to acid with constant stirring; stir while cooling until pearly sheen develops; perfume near 40 °C.
8. Advantages: non-greasy, matt, foundation base, washable. Disadvantages: little moisturising, alkaline soap may irritate, soaping effect, graininess on storage.
9. Comparison table: w/o vs o/w; beeswax-borax vs stearic acid-alkali; oily cooling vs dry matt; night/cleansing vs day/foundation.
10. Evaluation: pH, viscosity, spreadability, emulsion type, phase separation, microbial limits, irritation.

questions.answer:
1. Type: permanent (oxidation) hair dye; colour formed inside the hair cortex.
2. Ammonia (pH about 9–10) swells hair and opens cuticle so small colourless precursors enter.
3. Hydrogen peroxide oxidises p-phenylenediamine (primary intermediate) to reactive quinonediimine.
4. Quinonediimine reacts with couplers (resorcinol, m-aminophenol, 1-naphthol, m-phenylenediamine) to form large indo dyes (dimers, trimers) trapped in the cortex → permanent colour; different couplers give different shades; PPD self-coupling gives Bandrowski's base.
5. H2O2 also lightens natural melanin.
6. Other intermediates: p-toluenediamine, p-aminophenol.
7. Formulation – two parts mixed just before use: Part 1 dye cream/gel (PPD, couplers, ammonia or ethanolamine, surfactants, fatty alcohols, antioxidant sodium sulphite, chelating agent, conditioners, perfume); Part 2 developer (stabilised H2O2, acid, thickener, water).
8. Safety: PPD is a strong skin sensitiser causing allergic contact dermatitis; label warning; skin patch test about 48 hours before each use; not for eyebrows or eyelashes; gloves; 'black henna' with PPD causes severe reactions.
9. Evaluation: colour development, fastness to washing and light, shade uniformity, stability of both parts, pH, hair damage, sensitisation testing.

questions.answer:
1. Conditioning shampoo: cleans and conditions in one step. Building blocks: SLES 8–14% (primary surfactant), cocamidopropyl betaine (mildness), cationic polymer (polyquaternium-10, cationic guar), dimethicone emulsion, glycol distearate (pearlescence and suspension), NaCl (thickener), EDTA, citric acid (pH 5–6.5), preservative, perfume.
2. Mechanism: on dilution the cationic polymer–surfactant complex separates as a coacervate that deposits on negatively charged hair, carrying silicone → softness, easy combing, less static.
3. Hair conditioner: rinse-off product after shampoo. Building blocks: cationic surfactant (cetrimonium or behentrimonium chloride 1–3%), fatty alcohols (cetyl/stearyl 3–6%) forming lamellar gel network, silicones (dimethicone, amodimethicone), oils, proteins, panthenol, citric acid (pH 4–5, closes cuticle), preservative.
4. Method: melt fatty alcohol and cationic at 75 °C, add to hot water, cool slowly, add silicone and perfume below 40 °C. Types: rinse-off, leave-in, masks.
5. Anti-dandruff shampoo: cleansing base + active against Malassezia and scaling: zinc pyrithione, ketoconazole (drug), selenium sulphide, piroctone olamine, climbazole, salicylic acid, coal tar, herbal (tea tree, neem).
6. Formulation points: suspend insoluble actives evenly (acrylate polymers, glycol distearate), cationic polymers aid deposition, few minutes contact, suitable pH, conditioning to offset dryness.
7. Evaluation: pH, viscosity, foam, active content, combing tests, anti-dandruff efficacy (flake scoring), irritation, stability.

questions.answer:
1. Aim: restore and keep water in stratum corneum.
2. Mechanisms: occlusion (petrolatum, mineral oil, dimethicone), humectancy (glycerin, sodium PCA, hyaluronic acid), emolliency (esters, oils, fatty alcohols), barrier repair (ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids).
3. Typical o/w cream: oil phase – liquid paraffin/triglyceride 5–15%, cetostearyl alcohol 2–5%, emulsifier 2–5%, dimethicone 1–3%; water phase – glycerin 3–8%, EDTA, xanthan; cool-down – preservative, perfume, actives.
4. Method: heat both phases to 70–75 °C, homogenise, cool with stirring, add heat-sensitive items below 40 °C, adjust pH 5–6.
5. Advantages: hydration, vehicle for actives; disadvantages: comedogenic risk, emulsion instability, need for preservative.

questions.answer:
1. Cleanser for facial skin removing sebum, dirt and make-up without stripping.
2. Types: gel, foaming cream, lotion, foam, scrub, medicated (salicylic acid, tea tree oil).
3. Building blocks: mild anionic surfactant 8–15%, betaine 3–8%, glycerin 2–5%, carbomer 0.5–1.5%, EDTA, preservative, actives, pH adjusted to about 5.5–6.5, perfume, water.
4. Method: hydrate carbomer, add glycerin and EDTA, add surfactants gently, neutralise, add preservative/actives/perfume below 40 °C.
5. Advantages: milder and nearer skin pH than soap, easy to add actives, attractive.
6. Disadvantages: strong surfactants dry skin, needs preservative, short contact limits actives, scrub particles may irritate.

questions.answer:
1. Sensitivity: hydrodynamic theory – fluid movement in open dentine tubules stimulates nerve.
2. Desensitising agents: potassium nitrate/citrate (reduce nerve excitability); strontium chloride/acetate, stannous fluoride, arginine with calcium carbonate, calcium sodium phosphosilicate (occlude tubules); low-abrasion silica, fluoride; benefit builds over regular use.
3. Bleeding gums: usually gingivitis due to plaque.
4. Agents: antiplaque/antibacterial (stannous fluoride, zinc citrate, CPC), astringents (zinc salts, herbal tannins), herbal (neem, clove, miswak, aloe, turmeric); mild abrasive and surfactant.
5. Triclosan use has declined due to safety concerns.
6. Persistent bleeding needs a dentist.

questions.answer:
1. Whitening: surface stain removal by higher-cleaning abrasives (silica, calcium carbonate), enzymes, pyrophosphates; chemical bleaching by hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide (oxidise stain molecules) in gels, strips, trays; optical whitening by blue covarine.
2. Problems: sensitivity, gum irritation, enamel wear; strong bleaching under dentist.
3. Mouthwash: solution to rinse mouth for fresh breath, plaque and gingivitis control, fluoride.
4. Ingredients: antibacterial (chlorhexidine – can stain; CPC; essential oils thymol, eucalyptol, menthol, methyl salicylate), sodium fluoride, water/ethanol or glycols, glycerin/sorbitol, polysorbate, flavour, sweetener, preservative.
5. Use after brushing, rinse 30–60 s, spit out.

questions.answer:
1. Sunscreens: products that protect skin from UV radiation by absorbing, reflecting or scattering it.
2. UV bands: UVB 290–320 nm (sunburn, cancer), UVA 320–400 nm (tanning, photoageing, deep damage), UVC absorbed by ozone.
3. Chemical (organic) absorbers convert UV to heat: UVB – PABA and esters (padimate O), cinnamates (octinoxate), salicylates (octisalate, homosalate), octocrylene; UVA – benzophenones (oxybenzone), avobenzone, meradimate; newer broad spectrum (bemotrizinol, bisoctrizole).
4. Physical (inorganic) blockers reflect and scatter: zinc oxide, titanium dioxide (micronised).
5. Natural agents (aloe, green tea, curcumin) as supportive antioxidants; by form – lotions, creams, gels, sprays, sticks, water-resistant products.
6. Ideal properties: broad spectrum, photostable, non-irritant, water resistant, cosmetically acceptable, stable.
7. SPF = MED of protected skin ÷ MED of unprotected skin; MED = smallest UV dose giving just-visible redness after 16–24 h.
8. In vivo method: volunteers with fair skin, product at 2 mg/cm² on back, graded UV doses from solar simulator, read MED at 16–24 h; mean SPF; water resistance by re-testing after immersion.
9. In vitro: film on PMMA plate, spectrophotometric absorbance; Mansur equation SPF = CF × Σ EE × I × Abs (290–320 nm, CF 10).
10. Meaning: SPF 15 ≈ 93%, 30 ≈ 97%, 50 ≈ 98% UVB blocked. UVA rated by PA+ to PA++++ (persistent pigment darkening), UVA-PF, critical wavelength.
questions.question: What are sunscreens? Classify sunscreens with examples. Define SPF and describe its determination.

questions.answer:
1. Herbs are popular for tradition (Ayurveda), mildness, multiple actions and consumer preference; need standardisation, preservation and safety testing.
2. Aloe (Aloe vera leaf gel, Liliaceae/Asphodelaceae): polysaccharides (acemannan), amino acids, vitamins; moisturising, soothing, anti-inflammatory, burn healing; after-sun gels, moisturisers; aloin-containing latex removed; needs preservative.
3. Turmeric (Curcuma longa rhizome, Zingiberaceae): curcumin, turmerones; antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, brightening; face packs (ubtan), anti-acne creams, soaps; stains yellow, light- and alkali-sensitive.
4. Henna (Lawsonia inermis leaves, Lythraceae): lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone) binds keratin giving orange-red colour; hair dye and conditioner; with indigo for darker shades; black henna with PPD is dangerous.
5. Amla (Phyllanthus emblica fruit): vitamin C, tannins, flavonoids; antioxidant, astringent; hair oils, shampoos, packs to strengthen hair and reduce greying.
6. Neem (Azadirachta indica, Meliaceae): azadirachtin, nimbin, nimbidin; antibacterial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory; datun twigs, herbal toothpastes, mouthwashes, anti-acne and anti-dandruff products.
7. Clove (Syzygium aromaticum buds, Myrtaceae): eugenol; local anaesthetic, antiseptic, flavour; toothpastes, tooth powders, toothache products; undiluted oil irritates.
8. Limitations: variable composition, microbial load, colour and odour, allergy, limited evidence; claims must stay cosmetic.

questions.answer:
1. BIS publishes Indian Standards for cosmetics giving requirements and methods of test; Cosmetics Rules, 2020 require conformity where a standard exists.
2. Shampoo: description; pH of dilute solution; total non-volatile matter (dry at about 105 °C); active matter by two-phase titration with cationic titrant and mixed indicator; foam height and stability (cylinder shake, Ross–Miles); viscosity; surface tension; wetting time (canvas disc); dirt dispersion (Indian ink); cleaning of sebum from tresses; heavy metals (lead, arsenic); irritation; microbial limits; stability.
3. Skin cream: description; pH of aqueous dispersion; thermal stability (no separation at raised temperature); emulsion type (dilution, dye, conductivity); total fatty substance and non-volatile matter; viscosity and spreadability; globule size; heavy metals (no mercury); microbial limits; patch test; washability.
4. Toothpaste: description and consistency (continuous ribbon); pH of slurry; fineness of abrasive (wet sieving); sharp-edged particles (microscopy/scratch test); abrasivity; fluoride by ion-selective electrode (total not more than 1000 ppm in India); heavy metals; foaming; volatile matter; stability at raised temperature (no separation, tube corrosion); microbial limits; cleaning efficiency.
5. Purpose: consistent quality, consumer safety, label claims.

questions.answer:
1. Action: physical reflect, scatter (and partly absorb); chemical absorb UV and release heat.
2. Examples: ZnO, TiO2 vs PABA, cinnamates, salicylates, benzophenones, avobenzone, octocrylene.
3. Spectrum: physical broad (UVB, UVA, some visible); chemical depends on filter, combined for broad spectrum.
4. Appearance: physical may leave white cast (reduced by micronisation); chemical invisible.
5. Allergy: physical very low; some chemicals cause contact or photoallergy.
6. Photostability: physical stable; some chemicals degrade (avobenzone).
7. Suitability: physical for sensitive skin and children; chemical for daily cosmetic use.

4. In vitro: spectrophotometric absorbance of film or diluted product; Mansur equation over 290–320 nm.
5. SPF 15/30/50 block about 93/97/98% of UVB.
6. PA rating (PA+ to PA++++) indicates UVA protection, based on persistent pigment darkening.

questions.answer:
1. Purpose: prove claims (moisturising, oil control), check safety and guide formulation; non-invasive bioengineering.
2. General conditions: volunteers rest 15–30 min, room about 20–22 °C and 40–60% RH, baseline and control sites, repeated readings, statistics, consent.
3. Sebumeter: photometric grease-spot method; special opaque plastic tape pressed on skin for about 30 s; sebum makes tape transparent; light transmission measured by photocell; result µg/cm²; uses – skin typing, oil-control and anti-acne claims, scalp oiliness.
4. Corneometer: capacitance method; probe is a capacitor with conductor tracks under glass; stratum corneum acts as dielectric; water's dielectric constant about 80 vs below 7 for other substances; capacitance rises with hydration; arbitrary units; quick, superficial; uses – moisturiser efficacy, dryness after cleansing.
5. TEWL: water lost through epidermis (not sweat); marker of barrier function.
6. Open-chamber evaporimeter (Tewameter): two sensor pairs at different heights measure temperature and RH; vapour pressure gradient; Fick's law gives flux; g/m²/h; also closed-chamber and condenser methods.
7. Interpretation: damaged barrier (soap, surfactant, dermatitis) → high TEWL; occlusive and barrier-repair products lower it.
8. Precautions: no draughts, no sweating, probe still, stable readings.

questions.answer:
1. Soap: sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids made by saponification of fats/oils with alkali: triglyceride + 3 NaOH → 3 RCOONa + glycerol; sodium = hard, potassium = soft.
2. Evolution: fat heated with wood ash in ancient times → industrial alkali → milled toilet, transparent, medicated soaps → synthetic detergents and syndet bars to overcome high pH and hard-water scum.
3. Soap raw materials: tallow, palm, palm kernel, coconut oil, NaOH/KOH, glycerin, perfume, colour, antioxidant, EDTA, superfatting agents, TiO2.
4. Manufacture: saponification → glycerol separation → drying to noodles → amalgamation → milling → plodding → cutting, stamping, packing.
5. Quality: TFM; BIS grades 1/2/3 at least 76/70/60%; free alkali, moisture, alcohol-insoluble matter.
6. Soap problems: pH 9–10 disturbs acid mantle, removes lipids, raises TEWL, causes dryness and irritation; scum with hard water.
7. Syndet bar: synthetic surfactants – sodium cocoyl isethionate (main), sulphosuccinates, sulphoacetates; binders and plasticisers (stearic acid, fatty alcohols, starch), emollients, glycerin.
8. Combars: mixtures of soap and synthetic detergents.
9. Skin benefits of syndets: pH about 5.5–7, less lipid removal, lower TEWL, better hydration, less irritation; suitable for dry, sensitive, acne-prone, atopic and baby skin; no scum.
10. Comparison table: composition, pH, hard water, barrier effect, irritation, manufacture, wear, cost, suitability.
questions.question: What are soaps and syndet bars? Describe their evolution, composition and skin benefits with a comparison.

questions.answer:
1. Skin colour depends on melanin and haemoglobin; used for lightening, anti-tan, sunscreen, anti-redness claims and irritation scoring.
2. Mexameter (narrow-band reflectance): chosen wavelengths; melanin absorbs red, haemoglobin green → melanin index and erythema index.
3. Colorimeter/spectrophotometer: CIE L*a*b* – L* lightness, a* redness, b* yellowness/tan; ITA° from L* and b* grades skin tone.
4. Imaging with standard lighting and UV photography; visual grading.
5. Hair tensile strength: single fibre in tensile tester, stretched at constant rate until break (wet or controlled humidity); diameter measured first.
6. Stress–strain curve: Hookean region, yield region (helix unfolding), post-yield region, break; parameters – break stress, elongation at break, modulus, work to break; many fibres tested; bleached/permed hair weaker; fatigue testing.
7. Combing: standard hair tress on a load cell; comb drawn at constant speed; force vs distance; peak force and total combing work.
8. % reduction in combing work = (before − after) ÷ before × 100; wet combing for detangling, dry for smoothness and static.
9. Related: shine, friction, static, curl retention, sensory half-head tests.
questions.question: Describe the measurement of skin colour, hair tensile strength and hair combing properties in cosmetic evaluation.

questions.answer:
1. Measures casual sebum on the skin surface.
2. Special opaque plastic tape (about 0.1 mm) pressed on skin for about 30 s with constant pressure.
3. Sebum fills micro-pores and makes tape transparent (grease-spot effect).
4. Light passed through the tape; photocell measures transmission; more transmission = more sebum.
5. Result in µg/cm².
6. Uses: oily/dry skin typing, oil-control and anti-acne claims, sebum regrowth after washing.
7. Precautions: set time after washing, fixed contact time and pressure, controlled temperature.
questions.question: Explain the principle of the sebumeter.

questions.answer:
1. Measures hydration of the stratum corneum.
2. Probe is a capacitor: two conductor tracks covered by thin glass; no current passes into skin.
3. Skin acts as dielectric; water's dielectric constant (about 80) is much higher than other skin substances (below 7).
4. Capacitance rises with water content; read in arbitrary corneometer units.
5. Fast (about 1 s), measures only superficial layers, little affected by salts or residues.
6. Uses: moisturiser efficacy (short and long term), dryness after cleansers.
questions.question: Explain the principle of the corneometer.

questions.answer:
1. TEWL: water diffusing from inside the body through the epidermis and evaporating from the surface (not sweat); measure of barrier function.
2. Open-chamber evaporimeter: hollow cylinder on skin with two sensor pairs at different heights measuring temperature and relative humidity.
3. Vapour pressure gradient calculated; Fick's law gives water flux in g/m²/h.
4. Other methods: closed chamber, condenser chamber.
5. High TEWL = damaged barrier (soap, surfactants, dermatitis); occlusives and barrier repair lower it.
6. Precautions: no draught, rest, no sweating, controlled climate, probe held still.
questions.question: What is TEWL? How is it measured?

questions.answer:
1. Shows strength of hair and damage from bleaching, perming, dyeing, or protection by conditioners.
2. Single fibre, diameter measured, fixed between clamps of tensile tester with load cell.
3. Stretched at constant rate (wet or controlled humidity) until break.
4. Stress–strain curve: Hookean, yield, post-yield regions and break point.
5. Parameters: break stress, elongation at break, modulus, work to break.
6. Many fibres tested; damaged hair breaks at lower force; fatigue tests as variant.
questions.question: Explain the measurement of hair tensile strength.

questions.answer:
1. Bars made mainly of synthetic surfactants instead of soap.
2. Surfactants: sodium cocoyl isethionate, sulphosuccinates, sulphoacetates, acyl glutamates; binders and plasticisers (stearic acid, fatty alcohols, starch); emollients, glycerin, perfume.
3. pH about 5.5–7, close to skin.
4. Benefits: less removal of barrier lipids, lower TEWL, better hydration, less irritation and redness, no scum in hard water.
5. Suitable for dry, sensitive, acne-prone, eczema-prone and baby skin.
6. Drawbacks: costlier, harder to make, may wear faster or turn mushy. Combars combine soap and syndet.

questions.answer:
1. Sweat is nearly odourless; body odour comes from bacteria (Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus) breaking down apocrine secretions and sebum into volatile fatty acids, thioalcohols and steroid compounds.
2. Antiperspirant: reduces sweat amount; deodorant: reduces or masks odour; antiperspirant is an OTC drug in the USA, deodorant a cosmetic.
3. Antiperspirant actives: aluminium chlorohydrate (common, less acidic), aluminium zirconium chlorohydrate–glycine complexes (more effective, buffered, not in aerosols), aluminium chloride hexahydrate (strong, more irritant, for heavy sweating), activated salts.
4. Mechanism: salt dissolves in sweat → hydrolyses as pH rises in duct → aluminium hydroxide/polymeric gel precipitates with mucopolysaccharides → plug in upper eccrine duct → sweat blocked; cleared by skin renewal; also antibacterial.
5. Deodorant actives: antimicrobials (ethanol, chlorhexidine, quaternary ammonium compounds, farnesol, triclosan limited), odour absorbers (zinc ricinoleate, cyclodextrins), neutralisers (sodium bicarbonate, zinc oxide), enzyme inhibitors (triethyl citrate), perfume.
6. Forms: aerosols (anhydrous suspension in silicone + propellant or alcohol base), roll-ons, sticks (waxes + volatile silicone), creams, gels, powders.
7. Formulation points: even suspension, no nozzle blocking, quick drying, non-sticky, mildness, no white marks or stains.
8. Problems: irritation on shaved skin, stinging, fabric staining.
9. Evaluation: gravimetric sweat collection in hot room, odour assessment by trained sniffers, irritation testing.
questions.question: Discuss antiperspirants and deodorants: actives, mechanism of action and formulation.

questions.answer:
1. Blemishes: dark spots, post-inflammatory marks, melasma, freckles, sun spots; excess or uneven melanin from UV, inflammation, hormones; management – daily sunscreen, niacinamide, kojic acid, arbutin, liquorice, vitamin C, AHAs, cover make-up; hydroquinone and steroids are drugs, mercury not allowed.
2. Wrinkles: intrinsic ageing (thin skin, fine lines, less collagen and sebum) and photoageing (UVA, smoking, pollution – coarse wrinkles, solar elastosis); management – sunscreen, moisturisers, retinol, antioxidants, peptides, AHAs, niacinamide.
3. Acne: pilosebaceous disorder; increased sebum, follicular plugging (comedones), C. acnes, inflammation; aggravated by hormones, stress, comedogenic cosmetics; management – mild cleanser, non-comedogenic oil-free products, salicylic acid, niacinamide, tea tree, neem, clay; severe cases to dermatologist.
4. Prickly heat (miliaria): blocked eccrine ducts in hot humid weather → sweat leaks into skin → itchy red bumps; management – cool dry skin, cotton clothing, avoid heavy creams, prickly heat powder (talc, starch, zinc oxide, menthol, camphor), calamine.
5. Body odour: bacteria on apocrine secretions; puberty, heat, stress, hair, diet; management – washing, hair removal, cotton clothing, deodorants and antiperspirants.
questions.question: Describe the cosmetic problems associated with skin: blemishes, wrinkles, acne, prickly heat and body odour, with their causes and cosmetic management.

questions.answer:
1. Oily skin: high sebum, shine, enlarged pores, acne; causes – genetics, androgens, humid heat; care – gentle foaming cleanser, oil-free gel moisturiser, non-comedogenic products.
2. Dry skin: low barrier lipids and NMF; dull, rough, tight, flaky; care – mild cleanser, rich moisturiser.
3. Causes of dry skin: low humidity, cold wind, air conditioning, sun; hot water, frequent bathing, alkaline soaps; ageing; atopic tendency; hypothyroidism, diabetes, ichthyosis; drugs (retinoids, diuretics); nutrition; wet work and solvents.
4. Moisturisation: water held by intercellular lipids, NMF and sebum; moisturisers act by occlusion (petrolatum, dimethicone), humectancy (glycerin, urea, hyaluronic acid), emolliency (esters, oils), barrier repair (ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids), mild keratolytics; apply on damp skin; measured by corneometer and TEWL.
5. Comedogenic: ingredient or product that blocks pores forming comedones (blackheads open, whiteheads closed); examples – some esters (isopropyl myristate), lanolin derivatives, cocoa butter, heavy oils; non-comedogenic products tested to avoid this.
6. Dermatitis: skin inflammation – redness, itching, scaling; irritant contact (direct damage by surfactants, solvents) vs allergic contact (type IV to fragrance, preservatives, PPD); photo-contact, atopic, seborrhoeic; prevention by patch tests, fragrance-free products.
questions.question: Explain oily and dry skin, causes of dry skin and skin moisturisation. Add notes on comedogenic and dermatitis.

questions.answer:
1. Excess shedding of scalp skin as visible flakes, often with itching, without obvious inflammation (severe form seborrhoeic dermatitis).
2. Causes: Malassezia globosa and M. restricta; sebum broken by yeast lipase into irritant free fatty acids (oleic acid); individual sensitivity causing faster turnover.
3. Contributing: infrequent washing, stress, cold dry weather, hormones.
4. Management: anti-dandruff shampoos – zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine, climbazole, selenium sulphide, ketoconazole (drug), salicylic acid, coal tar, tea tree, neem.
5. Leave on scalp a few minutes; continue once or twice weekly to prevent return.
questions.question: What is dandruff? Discuss its causes and cosmetic management.

questions.answer:
1. Androgenetic alopecia: hereditary; DHT (via 5α-reductase) miniaturises follicles; male and female pattern.
2. Telogen effluvium: diffuse shedding 2–3 months after fever, illness, surgery, childbirth, crash dieting, stress, drugs.
3. Nutritional deficiency: iron, protein, zinc, biotin, vitamin D.
4. Hormonal and medical: thyroid disorders, PCOS, post-pregnancy, tinea capitis.
5. Alopecia areata: autoimmune patchy loss.
6. Drugs: anticancer drugs (anagen effluvium), some anticoagulants, retinoids.
7. Cosmetic and mechanical: traction from tight styles, bleaching, perming, straightening, heat, rough combing → breakage.
8. Approach: gentle care, avoid harsh treatment, nutrition, medical review for sudden or patchy loss.
questions.question: Write the causes of hair fall.

questions.answer:
1. Aim: antiperspirant reduces sweat; deodorant reduces or masks odour.
2. Actives: aluminium chlorohydrate, Al–Zr chlorohydrate glycine, aluminium chloride vs ethanol, antimicrobials, zinc ricinoleate, sodium bicarbonate, perfume.
3. Mechanism: gel plug of aluminium hydroxide in sweat duct vs killing bacteria, absorbing or masking odour.
4. Site: sweat glands vs bacteria and odour molecules.
5. Regulatory (USA): OTC drug vs cosmetic.
6. Irritation: more with aluminium salts on shaved skin vs mostly fragrance-related.
7. Often combined in one product.
questions.question: Differentiate between antiperspirants and deodorants.

questions.answer:
1. Disorder of the pilosebaceous unit, common in adolescents.
2. Factors: increased sebum (androgens), abnormal keratinisation and plugging (comedones), Cutibacterium acnes, inflammation (papules, pustules, nodules, cysts).
3. Aggravating: hormones, stress, comedogenic cosmetics, squeezing, some drugs.
4. Cosmetic care: mild cleanser twice daily, oil-free non-comedogenic moisturiser, salicylic acid, niacinamide, tea tree oil, neem, clay masks, remove make-up.
5. Benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics and retinoids are medicines; moderate/severe acne needs a dermatologist to prevent scarring.
questions.question: Write a note on acne and its cosmetic management.

questions.answer:
1. Prickly heat (miliaria): itchy, prickling tiny red or clear bumps in hot humid weather.
2. Cause: blocked eccrine sweat ducts; sweat leaks into skin and inflames it; common in babies, heavy sweaters, Indian summer.
3. Care: cool dry skin, loose cotton clothes, avoid heavy creams; prickly heat powders (talc/starch, zinc oxide, menthol, camphor), calamine.
4. Body odour: bacteria (Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus) break apocrine secretions into volatile fatty acids and thioalcohols.
5. Factors: puberty, heat, exercise, stress, hair, synthetic clothing, diet, hygiene.
6. Control: washing, hair removal, cotton clothing, deodorants and antiperspirants.
questions.question: Write a note on prickly heat and body odour.

questions.answer: A comedogenic ingredient or product tends to block hair follicles (pores) and cause comedones (blackheads and whiteheads).
questions.question: What is meant by comedogenic?

questions.answer: Aluminium chlorohydrate and aluminium zirconium chlorohydrate–glycine complex (also aluminium chloride hexahydrate).
questions.question: Name two antiperspirant actives.

questions.answer: Malassezia yeasts, mainly Malassezia globosa and Malassezia restricta.

# Unit 1: Cosmetics, cosmeceuticals, cosmetic excipients and the biology of skin, hair and mouth

Cosmetic science is the study of products that clean, protect and improve the look of the skin, hair, nails, lips and teeth. A pharmacist needs it because cosmetics are made in the same way as creams, lotions and gels, use the same excipients, and are controlled by the same law in India, the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. This unit gives the vocabulary for the rest of the subject: what a cosmetic is in law, how cosmeceuticals grew out of cosmetics, the excipients every formula is built from, and the basic biology of skin, hair and the mouth.

## 1.1 Definition of cosmetics as per Indian regulations

**Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.** In Indian law a **cosmetic** is any article meant to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, introduced into, or otherwise applied to the human body or any part of it, for **cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance**. The definition also covers any article meant to be used as a **component** of a cosmetic.

Key points in the Indian definition:

- The test is the **intended use** (the purpose and the claims made), not the chemical nature of the product.
- The word "introduced into" covers products such as mouthwashes and toothpastes.
- Ingredients sold for making cosmetics are themselves cosmetics in law.
- A product that claims to **treat, cure or prevent a disease** or to affect a body function is a **drug**, not a cosmetic, and needs a drug licence.

**Cosmetics Rules, 2020.** Until 2020 cosmetics were controlled through parts of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. In December 2020 the Central Government notified separate **Cosmetics Rules, 2020** under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. The main features students should know:

| Area | What the Rules cover |
| --- | --- |
| Authorities | The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), headed by the Drugs Controller General of India, acts as the Central Licensing Authority (import registration, new cosmetics); State Licensing Authorities issue licences to manufacture |
| Import | Cosmetics must be registered before import |
| Manufacture | A licence to manufacture for sale; premises, plant and hygiene requirements; a competent technical person; testing of raw materials and finished products |
| New cosmetic | A cosmetic containing a new ingredient (not used before) needs permission from the Central Licensing Authority |
| Standards | Cosmetics must meet the Indian Standards of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) where they exist; colours, preservatives and other ingredients must be from permitted lists and within limits |
| Labelling | Name of product, name and address of manufacturer, list of ingredients, batch number, date of manufacture, use-before date, net contents, directions and warnings where needed |
| Prohibitions | Misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics; testing of cosmetics on animals (banned in India since 2014) and import of cosmetics tested on animals after that ban |

**Misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics (in simple words):**

- **Misbranded:** coloured or packed to hide damage, or labelled falsely or not as the rules require.
- **Adulterated:** contains filthy or decomposed matter, prepared in insanitary conditions, has a non-permitted colour, or contains a harmful or toxic substance.
- **Spurious:** sold under another maker's name, imitates another product, or claims a manufacturer who does not exist.

Older textbooks refer to **Schedule M-II** (premises requirements for cosmetic factories) and **Schedule S** (BIS standards for cosmetics) of the 1945 Rules. These requirements now sit in the Cosmetics Rules, 2020.

## 1.2 Definition of cosmetics as per EU regulations

In the European Union cosmetics are controlled by **Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009**. A cosmetic product is any substance or mixture meant to be placed in contact with the **external parts of the body** (epidermis, hair, nails, lips, external genital organs) or with the **teeth and the lining of the mouth**, **only or mainly** to clean them, perfume them, change their appearance, protect them, keep them in good condition or correct body odour.

| Feature of EU law | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Responsible person | A named person in the EU is legally responsible for each product |
| Safety | A cosmetic product safety report (safety assessment) is required before sale |
| Notification | Every product is notified on a central EU portal before it is sold |
| Annexes | Lists of prohibited substances, restricted substances, permitted colourants, permitted preservatives and permitted UV filters |
| Animal testing | Testing finished cosmetics and ingredients on animals, and selling products so tested, is banned |
| Claims | Claims must be truthful and backed by evidence |

**Indian vs EU definition**

| Point | India (D&C Act, 1940) | EU (Regulation 1223/2009) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wording | Rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed, introduced or applied to the body | Placed in contact with external parts, teeth and oral mucosa |
| Purpose | Cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, altering appearance | Cleaning, perfuming, changing appearance, protecting, keeping in good condition, correcting body odour |
| Components | Included in the definition | Raw materials controlled through annexes |
| Pre-market step | Import registration or manufacturing licence | Safety report and portal notification |

## 1.3 Evolution of cosmeceuticals from cosmetics

A **cosmeceutical** is a product that sits between a cosmetic and a drug: it is applied like a cosmetic but contains an active ingredient claimed to give a real biological benefit, such as fewer wrinkles, even skin tone or better skin barrier. The word joins *cosmetic* and *pharmaceutical*. It was popularised by the American dermatologist **Albert Kligman**.

**How cosmetics evolved into cosmeceuticals:**

```text
Ancient cosmetics      → colour and cover (kohl, henna, turmeric, oils, clay)
Modern cosmetics       → emulsions, soaps, shampoos, lipsticks; mainly appearance
Functional cosmetics   → sunscreens, antiperspirants, anti-dandruff, fluoride toothpaste
Cosmeceuticals         → "active" skin and hair care: retinoids, AHAs, vitamin C,
                         niacinamide, peptides, antioxidants, botanical actives
```

Reasons for the growth of cosmeceuticals:

1. Better understanding of skin biology (barrier, ageing, pigmentation).
2. Demand for products that show visible results against ageing and pigmentation.
3. New delivery systems (liposomes, niosomes, nanoemulsions, microsponges) that carry actives into the upper skin.
4. Ageing populations and higher spending on personal care.
5. Dermatologists and pharmacies recommending such products.

**Common cosmeceutical actives**

| Group | Examples | Claimed benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retinoids | Retinol, retinyl palmitate | Smoother skin, fewer fine lines |
| Hydroxy acids | Glycolic acid, lactic acid (AHAs); salicylic acid (BHA) | Exfoliation, brighter skin, clearer pores |
| Vitamins and antioxidants | Ascorbic acid and derivatives, tocopherol, niacinamide, green tea polyphenols | Protection from oxidative damage, even tone |
| Peptides | Signal and carrier peptides | Support of collagen |
| Skin lighteners | Kojic acid, arbutin, liquorice extract, niacinamide | Less hyperpigmentation |
| Moisturising actives | Ceramides, hyaluronic acid, urea | Barrier repair, hydration |

**Legal status:** "cosmeceutical" is **not a legal category** in India, the EU or the USA. A product is either a cosmetic or a drug depending on its ingredients and claims. If a cosmeceutical claims to treat a skin disease, it must be licensed as a drug.

## 1.4 Classification of cosmetic and cosmeceutical products

**By site of use**

| Site | Products |
| --- | --- |
| Skin | Creams, lotions, face washes, soaps, sunscreens, face packs, powders, foundations, deodorants and antiperspirants |
| Hair and scalp | Shampoos, conditioners, hair oils, hair dyes, hair setting products, depilatories |
| Nails | Nail polish, nail polish remover, cuticle softeners |
| Lips | Lipsticks, lip balms |
| Eyes | Kajal, eyeliner, mascara, eye shadow |
| Oral cavity | Toothpastes, tooth powders, mouthwashes, teeth whitening products |

**By function:** cleansing (soaps, face washes, shampoos); protective (sunscreens, barrier creams); moisturising (moisturisers, cold creams); decorative or colour (lipstick, kajal, foundation, hair dyes); deodorising (deodorants, antiperspirants); fragrance (perfumes, colognes); corrective or cosmeceutical (anti-ageing, anti-acne, skin lightening).

**By physical form:** solutions (toners, mouthwash), emulsions (creams, lotions), gels, suspensions, powders, sticks (lipstick, deodorant stick), pastes (toothpaste), aerosols and sprays, bars (soap, syndet).

**Cosmeceutical classification by action:** anti-ageing, depigmenting, anti-acne, moisturising and barrier-repair, photoprotective, hair growth and anti-hair-fall.

## 1.5 Cosmetics as quasi drugs and OTC drugs

Some products do more than a plain cosmetic but are still sold freely. Different countries handle them differently.

- **Quasi drugs (Japan):** Japanese law has a middle category, "quasi drugs" (medicated cosmetics). Examples include medicated anti-dandruff shampoos, skin whitening products, anti-acne products, deodorants and hair growth products. They contain approved active ingredients at set amounts and need approval before sale, but are less strictly controlled than medicines.
- **OTC drugs (USA):** The US Food and Drug Administration treats a product as a drug if it is meant to treat or prevent disease or affect body structure or function. So **sunscreens, antiperspirants, anti-dandruff shampoos, fluoride toothpastes and anti-acne products** are over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, often with a cosmetic side as well (a "cosmetic–drug"). They must follow OTC rules for actives, strength and labelling.
- **India:** there is no separate quasi-drug class. A product with a disease claim (for example, an anti-dandruff shampoo with ketoconazole or a medicated toothpaste for gum disease) is licensed as a drug; the same type of product without such claims, using cosmetic ingredients, is a cosmetic.

| Product | Treated as (typical) | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plain moisturiser | Cosmetic everywhere | Appearance and feel only |
| Sunscreen | Cosmetic in India and EU; OTC drug in USA | Prevents sunburn |
| Antiperspirant | Cosmetic in India and EU; OTC drug in USA; quasi drug in Japan | Reduces sweating (a body function) |
| Fluoride toothpaste | Cosmetic in India and EU; OTC drug in USA | Prevents caries |
| Ketoconazole shampoo | Drug | Treats a fungal condition |

## 1.6 Cosmetic excipients

Excipients are the "building blocks" from which every cosmetic is made. The syllabus names five groups.

### Surfactants

Surfactants (surface active agents) have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. They lower surface and interfacial tension and are used to clean, foam, emulsify, wet, solubilise perfume and condition.

| Class | Head group charge | Examples | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anionic | Negative | Sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS), sodium laureth sulphate (SLES), soaps (sodium stearate), sodium cocoyl isethionate | Main cleansing and foaming agents in shampoos, face washes, toothpastes, bars |
| Cationic | Positive | Cetrimonium chloride, behentrimonium chloride, benzalkonium chloride | Hair conditioners (attach to negatively charged hair), antimicrobials |
| Amphoteric | Both (depends on pH) | Cocamidopropyl betaine, sodium lauroamphoacetate | Mild co-surfactants, baby shampoos, foam boosting |
| Non-ionic | No charge | Polysorbates, sorbitan esters, polyethylene glycol ethers of fatty alcohols, alkyl polyglucosides, cocamide DEA | Emulsifiers in creams, solubilisers for perfume, mild cleansers |

Choice depends on the job: anionics clean strongly but can irritate; amphoterics and non-ionics are milder; cationics condition but do not foam well. The **HLB** (hydrophilic–lipophilic balance) guides emulsifier choice: low HLB (about 3–6) for w/o creams, high HLB (about 8–18) for o/w creams and solubilisers.

### Rheology modifiers (thickeners)

They control viscosity, flow and stability (keeping particles and droplets suspended).

| Type | Examples | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural gums | Xanthan gum, guar gum, carrageenan, gum acacia | Lotions, toothpastes |
| Cellulose derivatives | Sodium carboxymethyl cellulose, hydroxyethyl cellulose, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose | Toothpaste, gels, shampoos |
| Synthetic polymers | Carbomers (crosslinked polyacrylic acid, thicken when neutralised) | Clear gels, face washes, lotions |
| Inorganic clays | Bentonite, magnesium aluminium silicate | Face packs, suspensions |
| Salt | Sodium chloride | Thickens shampoos based on ether sulphates |
| Fatty alcohols and waxes | Cetyl and cetostearyl alcohol, beeswax | Body for creams, sticks |

### Humectants

Humectants are hygroscopic substances that attract and hold water, both in the product (stop it drying out) and in the skin.

Examples: glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol, butylene glycol, sodium lactate, sodium PCA (pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, part of the skin's natural moisturising factor), urea, hyaluronic acid, honey. Limitation: in very dry air a humectant can pull water from the deeper skin, so it is usually combined with an occlusive or emollient.

### Emollients

Emollients soften and smooth the skin by filling gaps between surface cells and forming a thin film. Some also act as occlusives that reduce water loss.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Hydrocarbons | Liquid paraffin (mineral oil), petrolatum, squalane |
| Vegetable oils and butters | Almond, coconut, olive, sesame oils; shea and cocoa butter |
| Esters | Isopropyl myristate, isopropyl palmitate, caprylic/capric triglyceride |
| Fatty alcohols and acids | Cetyl alcohol, stearyl alcohol, stearic acid |
| Silicones | Dimethicone, cyclomethicone |
| Lanolin and derivatives | Wool fat, lanolin alcohols |
| Waxes | Beeswax, carnauba wax |

### Preservatives

Most cosmetics contain water, nutrients and are opened many times, so they need preservatives against bacteria, yeast and mould.

| Preservative | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Parabens (methyl, propyl) | Broad action, used together; methyl mainly against bacteria, propyl against fungi |
| Phenoxyethanol | Widely used, often with a booster |
| Benzoic acid / sodium benzoate, sorbic acid / potassium sorbate | Work best at acidic pH |
| Formaldehyde releasers (DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl urea) | Effective; can sensitise some users |
| Isothiazolinones | Very active at low levels; restricted because of skin allergy |
| Benzyl alcohol, dehydroacetic acid | Milder options |

**Ideal preservative:** broad spectrum, effective at low concentration, stable at product pH, compatible with other ingredients, non-irritant, no colour or smell, partitions enough into the water phase where microbes grow. Its effect is checked by a **preservative efficacy (challenge) test**.

Other excipients (antioxidants such as BHT and tocopherol, chelating agents such as disodium EDTA, pH adjusters, colours, perfumes) are covered with the products in Unit 2.

## 1.7 Skin: basic structure and function

The skin is the largest organ of the body. It has three layers.

```text
           Surface (stratum corneum, acid mantle pH about 4.5–5.5)
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ EPIDERMIS  (no blood vessels)                          │
 │   stratum corneum   – flat dead cells (corneocytes)    │
 │   stratum lucidum   – only in palms and soles          │
 │   stratum granulosum– granules, lipids made            │
 │   stratum spinosum  – "prickle" cells                   │
 │   stratum basale    – dividing cells, melanocytes      │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ DERMIS  papillary + reticular layers                   │
 │   collagen, elastin, fibroblasts, blood vessels,       │
 │   nerves, hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands   │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ HYPODERMIS (subcutis)  fat cells, larger vessels       │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Epidermis.** A stratified squamous epithelium. Cells (keratinocytes) are formed in the basal layer and move up, filling with keratin and losing their nuclei, until they become flat dead **corneocytes** that are shed. The journey takes roughly four weeks. The stratum corneum is the main **barrier**: often pictured as "bricks and mortar", with corneocytes as bricks and a lipid mortar of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids between them. It also holds the **natural moisturising factor (NMF)** (amino acids, PCA, lactate, urea) that keeps it supple. **Melanocytes** in the basal layer make **melanin**, which colours the skin and absorbs UV light. Langerhans cells take part in immune defence.

**Dermis.** Gives strength and elasticity through **collagen** (strength) and **elastin** (recoil) fibres in a gel of glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid, made by fibroblasts. Loss of these fibres with age and sunlight causes wrinkles.

**Hypodermis.** Fat that insulates, cushions and stores energy.

**Appendages:**

- **Sebaceous glands** – open into hair follicles; secrete **sebum** (triglycerides, wax esters, squalene, free fatty acids), which lubricates skin and hair. Most active on face, scalp, chest and back.
- **Eccrine sweat glands** – all over the body; watery sweat for cooling.
- **Apocrine sweat glands** – armpits and groin; become active at puberty; their secretion is broken down by bacteria to cause body odour.
- **Hair follicles** and **nails**.

**Functions of skin:** protection (mechanical, chemical, microbial, UV), barrier to water loss, temperature control (sweating, blood flow), sensation (touch, pain, heat), vitamin D synthesis, excretion (sweat), immune defence, absorption of some substances, and appearance and communication.

## 1.8 Hair: basic structure and growth cycle

A hair has a **shaft** (above the skin) and a **root** in the follicle, ending in the bulb around the **dermal papilla**, which supplies nutrients. The sebaceous gland and the arrector pili muscle are attached to the follicle.

```text
 Cross-section of a hair shaft
   ┌──────────────── cuticle (overlapping flat scales, protective)
   │  ┌───────────── cortex (long keratin cells, melanin; gives strength)
   │  │   ┌───────── medulla (loose central core; may be absent in fine hair)
   ○  ◎   •
```

- **Cuticle:** 6–10 layers of overlapping scales pointing to the tip; when flat and smooth, hair shines and combs easily. Damaged cuticle (by bleaching, heat, harsh shampoo) makes hair dull, rough and tangled.
- **Cortex:** the main bulk; long cells of **keratin**, a protein rich in cystine. Its strength comes from **disulphide bonds** (broken by perming and depilatory chemicals), **hydrogen bonds** (broken by water, reformed on drying — the basis of setting) and **salt (ionic) bonds** (affected by pH). The cortex holds the **melanin** that gives hair its colour.
- **Medulla:** a soft central core.
- Hair is weakly negatively charged at normal pH, which is why cationic conditioners stick to it.

**Hair growth cycle.** Each follicle cycles on its own, so hairs are not shed together.

| Phase | What happens | Approximate length | Share of scalp hairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anagen (growth) | Active growth from the bulb | 2–7 years on the scalp | About 85–90% |
| Catagen (transition) | Growth stops, follicle shrinks | About 2–3 weeks | About 1% |
| Telogen (resting) | Hair rests, then a new hair pushes it out | About 3 months | About 10–15% |
| Exogen (shedding) | The old hair falls | – | – |

Scalp hair grows about 1 cm a month. Shedding of up to about 100 hairs a day is usually normal. Hair fall disorders (Unit 5) often come from a change in this cycle, for example many hairs moving into telogen at once after illness or stress.

## 1.9 Oral cavity: common problems of teeth and gums

A tooth has **enamel** (hardest tissue, mainly hydroxyapatite) over **dentine** (with tiny tubules leading to the pulp), and a **pulp** with nerves and vessels. The gums (gingiva) cover the bone around the teeth.

| Problem | What it is | Cosmetic / oral care approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dental plaque | Sticky film of bacteria on teeth | Brushing, abrasives, antiplaque agents |
| Dental caries | Acids from bacterial fermentation of sugars dissolve enamel, causing cavities | Fluoride toothpaste, less sugar |
| Calculus (tartar) | Hardened (mineralised) plaque | Anti-tartar agents (pyrophosphates, zinc salts); scaling by a dentist |
| Gingivitis | Red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing, caused by plaque | Antiplaque and antibacterial toothpastes and mouthwashes |
| Periodontitis | Gum disease spreading to the bone, loosening teeth | Needs dental treatment |
| Dentine hypersensitivity | Sharp pain to cold, hot or sweet when dentine is exposed (worn enamel or receding gums) | Desensitising toothpastes |
| Tooth discolouration | Extrinsic stains (tea, coffee, tobacco) or intrinsic changes | Whitening toothpastes and bleaching |
| Halitosis | Bad breath, mainly from sulphur compounds made by bacteria on the tongue | Tongue cleaning, mouthwash |
| Mouth ulcers, dry mouth | Soft tissue problems | Mild mouthwashes; medical advice if persistent |

## Remember

- Indian definition: articles applied to the body to cleanse, beautify, promote attractiveness or alter appearance, including components (Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940).
- Cosmetics Rules, 2020 (December 2020) now control import, manufacture, labelling and sale of cosmetics; CDSCO is the Central Licensing Authority; states licence manufacture.
- EU: Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009; safety report, responsible person, notification, annexes, animal testing ban.
- A disease claim makes a product a drug. "Cosmeceutical" is not a legal category; the term was popularised by Kligman.
- Quasi drug = Japanese category; sunscreens, antiperspirants, anti-dandruff shampoos and fluoride toothpastes are OTC drugs in the USA.
- Five excipient groups: surfactants (anionic, cationic, amphoteric, non-ionic), rheology modifiers, humectants, emollients, preservatives.
- Skin: epidermis (5 layers, stratum corneum barrier, melanocytes), dermis (collagen, elastin, glands), hypodermis; acid mantle pH about 4.5–5.5.
- Hair: cuticle, cortex, medulla; keratin with disulphide, hydrogen and salt bonds; anagen → catagen → telogen → exogen.
- Oral problems: plaque, caries, calculus, gingivitis, periodontitis, hypersensitivity, stains, halitosis.
